newsitem.title: INDIA: Army asked to fight dengue fever in Indian capital.
newsitem.headline: Army asked to fight dengue fever in Indian capital.

text.p: The Indian army has been called in to help combat an epidemic of dengue fever in the Indian capital which has killed at least 126 people and infected more than 2,500, local authorities said on Monday.
Health officials said the epidemic had taken the largest toll of lives in 20 years in any single outbreak in the city.

Delhi Lieutenant-Governor P.K. Dave asked the army to open its hospitals to patients with dengue fever and to deploy units to spray areas of the capital where mosquitos which carry the disease breed, an aide to Dave said.
However, army officials said they had yet to receive an official request to help stop the spread of the disease, which health officials said had reached epidemic levels.
Dengue, a mosquito-borne disease which is also called breakbone fever, erupted in New Delhi in the last week of August during annual monsoons.

Accompanied by high fever, headaches and pain in muscles and joints, it normally runs its course in six to seven days. But a haemorrhagic form of dengue which can lead to internal bleeding and death has spread in the crowded capital.

"At least 126 persons have died in Delhi due to dengue fever and there were another 2,545 who reported sick to hospitals with the disease," said Vinod Jain of the city's Directorate of Health Services.
State officials said the administration was on a war footing, but health officers and doctors were generally critical of the decision to call in the army.
"It is primarily lip service," said Prem Aggarwal, general secretary of the Indian Medical Associaiton. "This is not the army's job, it is the work of the municipal authorities."
Aggarwal accused health planners of concentrating on building large hospitals instead of concentrating on improving basic sanitation as a means of combatting diseases.

"This is clearly a loss of priorities as most of the budget is spent on the creation of big hospitals rather than looking after the basic health necessities like potable water, cleanliness and sanitation," he said.
"Even if this disease is controlled, there will be another one. We need to clean the city rather than merely treat the patients," Aggarwal said.
The number of patients has strained hospital resources, prompting the request for army hospital beds.
There have been no reports of the disease spreading outside the capital.
"You cannot say the worst is over as the decline is still not in sight," said K.K. Dutta, director of the National Institute of Communicable Diseases.
Dutta said in February he sent guidelines to state governments on how to prevent diseases like dengue from spreading.
But he said no government had responded to his recommended steps.

"When they could have done something about it, they simply ignored it as it was not considered a public priority," he said. "But now when the situation has gone out of hand, it has become a priority."
